assignmentHtml.task: Research Apache Iceberg format details thoroughly. Investigate: (1) catalog implementations (HMS, REST, JDBC, Glue) and their role; (2) file formats — Parquet/ORC data files, manifest files, metadata files; (3) delete files — equality deletes vs position deletes, deletion vectors (V3/Puffin); (4) schema evolution and partition evolution mechanics; (5) time travel via snapshot IDs and timestamps; (6) concurrent writers and snapshot isolation; (7) what happens when a writer fails mid-commit; (8) compaction and expiring snapshots. Need production-grade understanding since the platform already has a 500TB Spark-written Iceberg lake.
assignmentHtml.context: Evidence cutoff 2026-09-16. Platform has existing 500TB Spark-written Iceberg lake on object storage with partition and schema evolution in use. Requirements include time travel, joins with operational data, selective access without copying. Need to explain catalog, file-format, delete-file, and concurrent-writer assumptions.
assignmentHtml.expected_output: Comprehensive Iceberg explanation covering catalog, file formats, delete files, time travel, concurrent writers, and failure behavior, with source URLs.

answerHtml:
Apache Iceberg is an open-table-format that manages large analytic datasets stored as immutable Parquet/ORC/Avro files in object storage, with all table state tracked in a layered metadata architecture. Below are detailed findings for each of the eight areas, tailored for a production platform running 500TB of Spark-written Iceberg data.

1. Catalog Implementations: HMS, REST, JDBC, Glue

The catalog is the table registry — it maps logical table names to current metadata file locations, provides atomic commit primitives (compare-and-swap), and enforces access control. It is never in the data path.

  • Hive Metastore (HMS): The original catalog. Stores only the table location and a metadata_location table property pointing to the current metadata.json in object storage. On every commit, the catalog implementation atomically updates metadata_location via a database transaction using compare-and-swap semantics. Readers query HMS for the pointer, then traverse the Iceberg metadata hierarchy in S3. Configuration: type=hive, uri=thrift://metastore-host:9083. Limitations: Thrift protocol is JVM-specific, no credential vending, limited RBAC, single point of failure risk, no branching/tagging. Best for teams already on HMS migrating from Hive tables; in-place migration is possible without copying data files.

  • REST Catalog: A vendor-neutral HTTP API (introduced in Iceberg 0.14, 2022) serving as the reference-standard catalog. Defines endpoints like GET /v1/{prefix}/namespaces/{ns}/tables/{table} (loads current metadata location + optional vended credentials) and POST .../tables/{table} (atomic commit). Supports OAuth2 auth, credential vending via cloud IAM (STS AssumeRole for S3, etc.), full RBAC (principal roles + catalog roles). Apache Polaris is the reference implementation. No JVM dependency, language-agnostic (Python, Go, Rust clients all work). Operational overhead includes managing the catalog service, ensuring availability, and OAuth2 infrastructure. Recommended for multi-engine deployments.

  • AWS Glue: Maps Iceberg namespaces → Glue Databases, tables → Glue Tables, and every table version → Glue TableVersion. Uses org.apache.iceberg.aws.glue.GlueCatalog with type=glue. Default warehouse location is my-warehouse/my_ns.db/my_table. Glue uses optimistic locking for concurrent updates. Best for AWS-native shops using Athena, EMR, Redshift, LakeFormation. IAM-based access control on Glue tables.

  • JDBC Catalog: Uses any relational database (PostgreSQL, MySQL) with atomic transactions to store Iceberg metadata. Requires the DB to support atomic transactions for serializable isolation commits. Configuration: type=jdbc, uri=jdbc:mysql://.... Easy to set up but provides no credential vending, no RBAC, no real multi-tenancy; typically used for development/testing, not production at scale.

For a 500TB platform, the catalog choice affects concurrency throughput and security posture. Glue and REST catalogs offer the best scalability with optimistic locking; HMS works but can become a bottleneck under high concurrency.

2. File Formats: Data Files, Manifest Files, Metadata Files

Iceberg is format-agnostic: it manages Parquet, ORC, and Avro data files while its own metadata files are stored as Avro (manifests, manifest lists) and JSON (table metadata).

Data Files (Parquet/ORC/Avro): Immutable files containing all column values, including partition columns even if redundant with manifest metadata (providing a backup against metadata corruption). Each data file record is tracked in manifests with:

  • file_path (full URI), file_format, partition_spec_id, data_sequence_number, record_count, file_size_in_bytes
  • Column-level statistics: column_sizes, value_counts, null_value_counts, nan_value_counts, lower_bounds, upper_bounds (keyed by field ID, not name)
  • sort_order_id and estimated_size/existing_columns metrics

Manifest Files (immutable Avro): Each lists data files or delete files with status (0=EXISTING, 1=ADDED, 2=DELETED), snapshot_id, sequence_number, and a nested data_file struct. One or more manifests constitute a snapshot. Query engines prune files using partition summaries and column statistics before reading.

Manifest List (immutable Avro, one per snapshot): Lists all manifests belonging to a snapshot, with per-manifest metadata including partition_spec_id, sequence_number, min_sequence_number, and partition value ranges (min/max) for data skipping. Snapshot chaining: each snapshot references a manifest list and has parent_snapshot_id, creating a linear history.

Table Metadata JSON (*.metadata.json): The single source of truth for table state:

  • format-version (1, 2, or 3), table-uuid, location
  • last-updated-ms, last-sequence-number, last-column-id
  • schemas (list with schema-id), current-schema-id
  • partition-specs (list with spec-id), default-spec-id
  • sort-orders, default-sort-order-id
  • properties (table configurations)
  • snapshots (list: snapshot-id, timestamp-ms, manifest-list, summary with operation stats)
  • current-snapshot-id, snapshot-log (history of current snapshot changes), metadata-log (path + timestamp of previous metadata files)

On every commit, a new metadata file is written and the pointer is swapped atomically — old files remain for time travel until expired.

3. Delete Files: Equality vs Position Deletes, Deletion Vectors (V3/Puffin)

Row-level deletes are stored in separate delete files, applied at read time (Merge-on-Read).

  • Equality Delete Files (V1+): Identify deleted rows by column values matching (id = 5), e.g., from DELETE WHERE statements. Applied when the data file's data_sequence_number is strictly less than the delete file's sequence number and partitions match. May optionally include additional columns of the deleted row. Still the primary delete mechanism in all versions.

  • Position Delete Files (V2): Identify deleted rows by file_path + row position within the file (a row may optionally be included). Applied when the data file's data_sequence_number is less than or equal to the delete file's, and the data file's partition equals the delete file's. Deprecated in V3 — existing position deletes must be converted to deletion vectors when updating.

  • Deletion Vectors (V3, stored in Puffin files): The V3 innovation. Instead of enumerating row positions in verbose Parquet, deletion vectors encode deleted row positions as compressed bitmaps (deletion-vector-v1 blob definition in Puffin). Multiple vectors can coexist in a single Puffin file per data file. Key properties:

    • Only one deletion vector may exist per data file — new deletes merge into the existing vector rather than creating new files
    • Vectors are applied based on sequence numbers: a position delete file/vector must be applied when the data file's data sequence number ≤ the delete's data sequence number
    • Measured improvements (EMR, Iceberg 1.9.2): 55% faster delete operations, 73.6% smaller delete file storage (1801→475 bytes), 28.5% faster full reads, 23% faster filtered reads
    • As of the evidence cutoff, Spark is the only fully supported engine for deletion vectors
    • Compaction (rewrite_data_files) can remove deleted rows entirely from data files, eliminating pending delete application

Application rules (from the spec): Engines apply delete files to a data file only when sequence numbers and partition specs align, ensuring correctness without global ordering assumptions.

4. Schema Evolution and Partition Evolution Mechanics

Both are metadata-only operations — no data files are rewritten.

Schema Evolution supports: Add (new column at top level or in nested struct), Drop (remove column), Rename, Update (widen types: int→long, float→double, decimal(P,S)→decimal(P',S) where P'>P), and Reorder columns. Correctness guarantees:

  1. Added columns never read existing values from another column
  2. Dropping a column doesn't change other columns' values
  3. Updating doesn't change other columns
  4. Reordering doesn't change which values belong to which name

This is achieved through unique field IDs assigned per schema version. All formats store field IDs in the file schema (Parquet: field IDs on the schema; Avro: field-id properties). Projection at read time uses field IDs, not names or positions, so existing data files remain readable after any evolution. Each schema gets a unique schema-id; the list of schemas is retained in table metadata. Renaming does not break the layout because the field ID stays constant.

Partition Evolution: Partition specs can be evolved by adding, removing, renaming, or reordering partition fields. Changes produce a new spec-id added to partition-specs. Critical constraint: partition field IDs should not change during evolution because manifest files use partition field IDs as partition tuple field IDs. Old data retains its original spec; new data is written under the new spec. Because partitioning is "hidden" (queries don't reference partition layouts directly), Iceberg performs split planning — each partition layout plans files separately using filters derived for that specific layout. Both layouts coexist seamlessly.

Sort order evolution follows the same pattern via replaceSortOrder(), though old data remains unsorted unless explicitly rewritten.

5. Time Travel via Snapshot IDs and Timestamps

Every write produces a new snapshot recorded in table metadata with snapshot-id, timestamp-ms, manifest-list, and summary (operation, added/total records and files). Snapshots form a linear history via parent_snapshot_id.

Query mechanisms (Spark SQL):

  • VERSION AS OF <snapshot_id> — selects a specific snapshot; uses that snapshot's schema
  • TIMESTAMP AS OF '2025-01-01 10:00:00' or Unix seconds — selects the snapshot current at that time; uses that snapshot's schema
  • VERSION AS OF 'branch_name' — head of branch; uses the table's current schema (rows written before the branch point get NULL for newly added columns)
  • VERSION AS OF 'tag_name' — tag-bound snapshot; uses the snapshot's schema
  • Identifier forms: table.branch_<name>, table.tag_<name>
  • DataFrame API: options snapshot-id, as-of-timestamp (ms), branch, tag
  • Incremental reads: start-snapshot-id (exclusive), end-snapshot-id (inclusive) — append-only, not available in SQL

Time travel also applies to metadata tables (table.snapshots, table.history, table.manifests, table.files, table.partitions).

A key nuance: branches use the table's current schema (new columns appear as NULL for older rows), while tags/snapshot IDs use the historical snapshot schema. This matters for join compatibility with operational data.

6. Concurrent Writers and Snapshot Isolation

Iceberg implements optimistic concurrency control (OCC) with atomic compare-and-swap commits, providing serializable isolation by default.

Write transaction flow:

  1. Read current table state (optional for appends)
  2. Determine changes, write new data files
  3. Load latest metadata, determine base metadata version
  4. Data conflict check — validate compatibility with the latest snapshot
  5. Generate new metadata files
  6. Commit — CAS swap of the metadata pointer. On failure, retry from step 3 (only the metadata portion is re-done, not the full transaction)

Two conflict types:

  • Catalog commit conflicts (transient, auto-retried): Multiple writers attempt the atomic swap simultaneously. Retried based on table properties (commit.retry.num-retries, min-wait-ms, max-wait-ms, total-timeout-ms). Recommended: 10 retries for streaming ingestion, 4 for compaction. On exhaustion → CommitFailedException.
  • Data update conflicts (non-retryable by library): Detected during validation when concurrent transactions modify overlapping data (e.g., two writers logically deleting the same file). Fails with ValidationException; requires custom retry logic with exponential backoff.

Isolation levels:

  • Serializable (default): All validation checks enabled, including "Added data files validation" — prevents a concurrent operation from adding data matching another's pushed-down predicate
  • Snapshot Isolation (weaker, faster): Enables all checks except added-data-file validation. For streaming-vs-compaction conflicts, offers no benefit over serializable.

Configured per operation: write.delete.isolation-level, write.update.isolation-level, write.merge.isolation-level.

Operation-specific conflict checks:

  • APPEND: No checks (no primary keys, duplicates allowed)
  • OverwriteFiles (COW): Fail-missing-delete-paths, no-new-deletes, added-data-file validation
  • RowDelta (MoR): Data-files-exist, no-new-delete-files, added-data-files validation
  • RewriteFiles (compaction): Fail-missing-delete-paths, no-new-deletes (always enabled)

7. What Happens When a Writer Fails Mid-Commit

The design guarantees atomicity through the metadata pointer swap: either the commit succeeded (new metadata is visible) or nothing changed (the old metadata persists). There is no intermediate state visible to readers.

Specific scenarios:

  • Failure after writing data files but before commit: The writer's data files exist in storage unreferenced by any snapshot — these become orphan files. The table state is untouched. The job can be retried from the current state. Orphan cleanup (remove_orphan_files) later deletes them via set-difference between all files under the table location and files reachable from metadata.
  • Failure during commit (network error, timeout): The CAS fails or hangs. The failed writer's metadata tree is discarded. On retry, the writer reloads current metadata and rebuilds its changes. Since appends create new manifest files that can be reused across retries, the cost of retry is mostly metadata, not re-reading data.
  • Committed but orphaned metadata files: With write.metadata.delete-after-commit.enabled=true, Iceberg deletes the oldest tracked metadata file when writing a new one, keeping the metadata log bounded. A metadata file falling out of the log without deletion becomes an orphan (found only by orphan cleanup, default retention 3 days).
  • Orphan files from lost commit conflicts: Normal in OCC — the losing writer's data files become orphans. This is expected behavior, not a bug.

Critical safety note: orphan cleanup compares path strings and requires a full storage listing. The older_than window (default 3 days) must exceed the longest write duration, otherwise in-flight files get deleted and corrupt the table. Always run dry_run first, especially on a 500TB lake.

8. Compaction and Expiring Snapshots

These are the two pillars of Iceberg table maintenance, executed via Spark procedures.

Compaction (rewrite_data_files):

  • Combines small data files into optimally sized ones (target default 512MB, configurable via target-file-size-bytes)
  • Strategies: binpack (simple packing, fastest), sort (linear sort), zorder(c1,c2) (multi-column space-filling curve)
  • Applies pending position and equality deletes into the rewritten files, producing clean output with no pending delete application
  • Rewrites manifests to reduce metadata overhead
  • Options: min-input-files (default 5), min-file-size-bytes/max-file-size-bytes (75%/180% of target), max-file-group-size-bytes (100GB default, splits very large partitions), where predicate filtering, partial-progress.enabled (commits groups incrementally), remove-dangling-deletes (removes delete files referencing no live data)
  • File groups are split by partition and size; max-concurrent-file-group-rewrites (default 5) controls parallelism
  • Also available: rewrite_position_delete_files for minor compaction of delete files + dangling delete removal

Expiring Snapshots (expire_snapshots):

  • Removes old snapshots and their uniquely-referenced data files (never removes files still needed by non-expired snapshots)
  • Arguments: older_than (default 5 days ago), retain_last (default 1 ancestor), snapshot_ids
  • Branches/tags referencing snapshots prevent expiration unless history.expire.max-ref-age-ms is set; the main branch never expires
  • Outputs counts of deleted data files, delete files, manifests, manifest lists, and statistics files
  • Must run before orphan cleanup in the maintenance sequence

Recommended maintenance sequence: compact data files → rewrite manifests → expire snapshots → remove orphan files. Run orphan cleanup monthly and after compaction/expiry. For a 500TB lake, consider partition-level targeting via where predicates and Z-order strategies aligned with query patterns to maximize benefits.

Key Production Considerations for Your Platform

  1. Your 500TB Spark-written lake likely uses Parquet with V1/V2 format. Consider upgrading to V3 for deletion vectors if Spark versions support it.
  2. Field IDs in your existing data files enable schema evolution without rewriting — this is a free capability.
  3. Concurrent writes via OCC will produce occasional CommitFailedException on hot tables; configure retry properties appropriately.
  4. Orphan file cleanup is expensive (full listing of 500TB); use dry_run and consider prefix_listing for performance.
  5. Snapshot expiration must respect your SLA for time travel — expired snapshots cannot be recovered.
  6. Delete file accumulation degrades read performance; plan compaction cycles around delete volume.

evidence.snippet: Official Iceberg Table Spec — defines data file fields, manifest/manifest list structures, delete file types (position vs equality), deletion vector V3 encoding, schema/partition evolution rules, sequence number application rules for deletes
evidence.supports: File format structures, delete file mechanics, schema/partition evolution, and delete application rules are all defined in the spec with precise field definitions and conditions

evidence.snippet: Schema evolution supports add/drop/rename/update(re widen)/reorder as metadata-only changes with four correctness guarantees enforced via unique field IDs. Partition evolution creates new spec IDs, keeps old data unchanged, enables split planning. Hidden partitioning means queries don't reference layouts directly.
evidence.supports: Schema and partition evolution mechanics, field-ID-based projection, and split planning behavior

evidence.snippet: Time travel via TIMESTAMP AS OF, VERSION AS OF (snapshot id, branch, tag), FOR SYSTEM_TIME/SYSTEM_VERSION, DataFrame options snapshot-id/as-of-timestamp/branch/tag. Snapshot schema vs table schema selection differs by clause type. Metadata tables support time travel too.
evidence.supports: Time travel mechanisms, schema selection nuances, incremental read, and metadata table time travel

evidence.snippet: Serializable isolation via linear history of atomic table updates. Optimistic concurrency: writers assume no conflicts, atomically swap metadata, retry on conflict by rebuilding metadata tree from new current state. Work structured for reuse across retries. Assumptions-and-actions validation before re-applying actions.
evidence.supports: Concurrent writer model, serializable isolation, retry mechanics, and failure handling

evidence.snippet: CAS commit requires current metadata location match. Four operation types: APPEND (no checks), OVERWRITE/COW (fail-missing-delete-paths, no-new-deletes, added-data-file validation), RowDelta/MoR (data-files-exist, no-new-delete-files, added-data-files), RewriteFiles/compaction (fail-missing-delete-paths, no-new-deletes). Snapshot isolation enables all checks except added-data-file; Serializable enables all.
evidence.supports: Detailed data conflict checks per operation type and isolation level differences

evidence.snippet: Catalog commit conflicts auto-retried with table properties (commit.retry.num-retries etc.); data update conflicts fail with ValidationException requiring custom handling. Serializable (default) vs Snapshot isolation. Write pattern conflict matrix: INSERT always retryable-commit-conflict, never data-conflict; UPDATE/DELETE and Compaction can have both.
evidence.supports: Conflict types, retry configuration, isolation level settings, and write-pattern-specific conflict likelihood

evidence.snippet: Orphans are files written but never committed — residue of failed/killed tasks and lost commit conflicts. Cleanup is a set difference between all files under table location and files reachable from metadata. Requires full storage listing. older_than default 3 days; shorter than write duration risks deleting in-flight files. Path string comparison risks; dry_run essential.
evidence.supports: Orphan file causes, detection algorithm, safety requirements, and cleanup procedure details

evidence.snippet: Full procedure specifications for expire_snapshots (older_than, retain_last, snapshot_ids, clean_expired_metadata), remove_orphan_files (older_than, dry_run, equal_schemes, prefix_mismatch_mode), rewrite_data_files (strategy binpack/sort, target/min/max file sizes, min-input-files, max-file-group-size-bytes, partial-progress, remove-dangling-deletes, delete-ratio-threshold), rewrite_manifests, rewrite_position_delete_files.
evidence.supports: Complete compaction and maintenance procedure parameters, defaults, and options

evidence.snippet: Compaction rewrites small data files to 128-512MB targets, applies pending deletes into clean files, rewrites manifests. Streaming micro-batches can produce 2,880 files/day/partition. Binpack/sort/Z-order strategies. Delete file accumulation forces join-like operations at read time.
evidence.supports: Compaction rationale, mechanics, strategies, and delete file application during compaction

evidence.snippet: REST Catalog (Iceberg 0.14+) is vendor-neutral HTTP API with OAuth2, credential vending via cloud IAM, full RBAC (Polaris reference impl). HMS uses Thrift/JVM-only, no vending. Glue is AWS-only proprietary. JDBC is dev/test-oriented. Comparison table with protocol, vending, RBAC, engine support per catalog type.
evidence.supports: Catalog landscape, REST advantages, and trade-offs for each catalog implementation

evidence.snippet: Glue catalog maps namespaces→Databases, tables→Glue Tables, versions→TableVersions. Uses optimistic locking. Default warehouse in S3 via S3FileIO. glues.id property for cross-account. Recommended for AWS analytics ecosystem, high-throughput apps with optimistic locking, IAM-based access control.
evidence.supports: AWS Glue catalog implementation details, mapping, and recommended use cases

evidence.snippet: HMS stores table location + metadata_location property; atomic updates via database transaction with CAS semantics. Readers query HMS for metadata_location then traverse object storage. In-place Hive migration possible without copying data. Limitations: JVM-only Thrift, no credential vending, DB bottleneck, SPOF, no branching.
evidence.supports: HMS catalog mechanics, atomic commit primitive, limitations, and migration path

evidence.snippet: JDBC catalog uses relational DB (PostgreSQL/MySQL) with atomic transactions for serializable isolation commits. Configured via uri + jdbc.* properties. No credential vending or RBAC; typically dev/test only.
evidence.supports: JDBC catalog implementation and appropriate scope

evidence.snippet: V3 deletion vectors use compressed bitmaps in Puffin files instead of verbose Parquet position delete files. Binary DVs reduce I/O, allow multiple vectors per Puffin file, enable continuous merging. EMR benchmark: 55% faster deletes, 73.6% smaller files (1801→475 bytes), 28.5% faster full reads, 23% faster filtered reads. As of test, Spark is the only supported engine.
evidence.supports: Deletion vector mechanics, Puffin format, and measured performance improvements over V2 position deletes

evidence.snippet: Metadata.json mandatory fields: format-version, table-uuid, location, last-sequence-number, last-updated-ms, last-column-id, schemas (with schema-id), current-schema-id, partition-specs (with spec-id), default-spec-id, sort-orders, default-sort-order-id, properties, snapshots (snapshot-id, timestamp-ms, manifest-list, summary), current-snapshot-id, snapshot-log, metadata-log.
evidence.supports: Complete table metadata.json structure and all required fields
